title: Are They Kind
author: Lynsey White
summary: A school leader writes about watching her own daughter start secondary school and finding that the experience rearranged her sense of what school culture actually is. The frame is the question her family asks at the end of every day, were they kind, and the answers her daughter brings home: staff who greet her off the bus, a teacher who already knows her name, every adult who passes her in reception stopping to check in. White's argument is that these are not soft extras layered over the real work of schooling but the substance of it, and she contrasts them deliberately with tracking, top sets, inspection performance and culture initiatives. A second episode sharpens the point: a Year 7 boy taps her shoulder to ask where he can play, adding that his mother told him to ask for help, and the three minutes she spends helping him become her illustration of how much a small interaction carries for a child. The piece closes as a call to leaders to treat warmth as mission-critical and to hold colleagues to account on it. Its value as a document is the leader-as-parent vantage point, which lets her describe the invisible architecture of a school day from the receiving end.
points: The organising device is a standing family question, were they kind, which White treats as a sharper diagnostic of a school than attainment data.
She lists the specific micro-moments her daughter reports, greetings off the bus, praise points, a headteacher calling her a legend, as evidence that culture is transmitted person by person.
The reception anecdote turns on the fact that a child sitting quietly for thirty minutes could easily become part of the furniture and instead was noticed by every passing adult.
A lost Year 7 saying his mother told him to ask for help becomes her case that stepping into school takes courage and depends on adult warmth.
Her conclusion refuses the framing of warmth as an initiative or an inspection performance and instead names it as the work itself.
quotes: As a school leader, you spend years knowing the theory, reading the frameworks, and talking about culture until it feels like a second language.
All summer long, my mind wasn't racing about academic tracking or top sets. Instead, it was entirely consumed by the micro-moments.
But beyond the usual chatter about her lessons, there is one question that is a non-negotiable family routine: "Were they kind?
A child sitting quietly in reception could easily become part of the furniture.
They aren’t putting on a show for an inspector. They aren’t ticking a box. They aren’t delivering a “culture initiative”. They are just being brilliantly, relentlessly human.
Today, a small hand tapped me gently on the shoulder. I turned to find a Year 7 boy looking a little lost. In a small, quiet little voice, he asked, "Where can I play?
It was a poignant reminder of the courage it takes for these children to step into our world every single day, relying entirely on our safety and warmth.
We sometimes talk about warmth as if it is something that sits around the edges of the “real work” of education.
